Cho-Gochujang Sweet-Tangy Chili Sauce

Cho-gochujang — "vinegar gochujang" — is the bright member of the dip family: gochujang loosened and sharpened with vinegar and sweetener into a spooning-and-dunking sauce that runs where ssamjang (#SA01) sits.

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — vinegar's bowl. Cho-gochujang — "vinegar gochujang" — is the bright member of the dip family: gochujang loosened and sharpened with vinegar and sweetener into a spooning-and-dunking sauce that runs where ssamjang (#SA01) sits. It is the classic partner for raw and chilled things — cold noodles, cucumber, hwe-style seafood — and at the grill table it is the bowl for anything that wants sweetness cut with a real acid line: the shrimp records, the squid (#SF04), skewers (#M18). One bowl, ten minutes, and the vinegar does the transforming.

The sauce

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The order: dissolve the sweet in the sour before the paste joins. Vinegar and honey whisked until clear, then the gochujang worked in — this direction dissolves the paste smoothly; the reverse direction chases lumps.
  • Loosen to the target use: a spooning sauce for noodles and cucumber runs thicker (barely falling from the spoon); a dunking bowl for grilled pieces runs looser (another tablespoon of water). Decide the bowl's job before the last splash.
  • Taste after the sesame oil, before the build-ins: it should read sweet-and-sour first, fermented-warm second — like a Korean sweet-chili sauce that went to school. Sharper or sweeter is a teaspoon of vinegar or honey away.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Vinegar, honey, and water whisked clear; gochujang in, worked to one even red-orange with no dark streaks. Checkpoint — a spoon dragged through leaves a slowly-closing trail — the thickness of thick honey for the noodle build.
  2. 02
    Garlic, sesame oil, sesame seeds; the build-ins to the bowl's job; a final taste — the vinegar should be present on the finish of a dipped finger, a clean snap after the sweet. Checkpoint — the eating test on a piece of plain cucumber: snap, sweet, heat hum, acid line. If the cucumber tastes pickled in ten seconds of sitting, the vinegar ran a splash heavy; if it reads as plain gochujang, the vinegar is shy. Chef’s Note — cho-gochujang is the Korean table's most under-exported sauce, and the reason is a translation problem: it is not "Korean sweet chili sauce" — the commercial sweet-chili in a squeeze bottle is sugar and starch with chili, while cho-gochujang is a fermented paste loosened by acid, which is why it has depth where the bottled one has only sweetness. The two are not interchangeable in either direction. Ten minutes and five shelf staples buys the real bowl.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Lumpy pasteSweet and paste whisked dry-firstVinegar-and-honey first, paste second
Too sweet, flatHoney-forward balanceVinegar by the teaspoon until the snap arrives
One-note hotGochugaru plus a hot gochujang jarSkip the gochugaru; more honey
Thickened in the fridgeCold tightens the pasteA splash of water and a stir at serving

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 1 week refrigerated and genuinely improves on days two and three as the vinegar mellows into the paste. Cucumber build-ins go in at serving, not storage.
  • Variations: the raw-seafood build with pear slivers; a spoon over the jjukkumi record (#SF06) instead of the marinade for a lighter tent; thinned further with water and a drop of soy, it dresses the cold noodle bowls and the squid's leftovers.
